title: Clinical and Patient-Centered Outcomes of Catheter Ablation According to Symptom Status in Very Elderly Patients With Atrial Fibrillation: A Subgroup Analysis of the REHEALTH AF Registry.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Catheter ablation can improve symptoms and functional status in very elderly patients with atrial fibrillation. However, it is uncertain if baseline symptom status can pinpoint those who will benefit the most.

METHODS: This exploratory subgroup analysis examined data from the REHEALTH AF registry, which included patients aged 80 and above with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Patients were categorized by baseline symptom status and compared based on treatment strategy: catheter ablation versus non-ablation management.

RESULTS: Of 703 patients, 238 were asymptomatic, while 465 were symptomatic. Catheter ablation did not significantly reduce the primary composite endpoint in either asymptomatic (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.39; 95% confidence interval, 0.39-4.92; p = 0.61) or symptomatic patients (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.66; 95% confidence interval, 0.36-1.20; p = 0.17), with no significant interaction between treatment and symptoms. Exploratory analyses indicated ablation was associated with more favorable changes in a wider range of 1-year patient-centered measures among symptomatic patients, such as quality of life, self-rated health, Mini-Mental State Examination score, frailty distribution, N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level, and left atrial diameter. In asymptomatic patients, improvements were mainly seen in self-rated health and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide level.

CONCLUSIONS: In very elderly patients with atrial fibrillation, baseline symptom status did not identify those with a clear short-term event reduction following catheter ablation. Nevertheless, exploratory analyses revealed more favorable changes across various patient-centered measures in symptomatic patients, although formal evidence of effect modification was limited.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: University Hospital Medical Information Network Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000047023.

title: The Impact of Preoperative Atrial Fibrillation on Outcomes Following Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation.
summary: A preoperative history of atrial fibrillation (AF) in patients receiving durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation has been associated with postoperative morbidity and mortality. It is uncertain how the type of preoperative AF (paroxysmal vs. persistent/permanent) impacts clinical outcomes in patients on LVAD support. We sought to determine how the presence and type of preoperative AF affect patient mortality following LVAD implantation. A single-center retrospective analysis was performed of patients who underwent LVAD implantation from 2006-2022. Patients with AF prior to LVAD implantation were characterized as having paroxysmal or persistent/permanent AF for comparison. A total of 289 patients (37%) with a history of preoperative AF underwent LVAD implantation. Paroxysmal AF (78.9%) was more common prior to LVAD implant than persistent/permanent AF (21.1%). The incidence of 30-day and 2-year all-cause mortality were significantly higher amongst patients with preoperative persistent/permanent AF compared to patients without reoperative AF (30-day mortality: 16.4% vs 6.4%, p=0.005; 2-year all-cause mortality: 44.3% vs 24.2%, p=0.001). Over long-term follow-up, the risk of all-cause mortality was significantly higher for patients with preoperative persistent/permanent AF compared to patients without preoperative AF controlling for age, sex, race, class III antiarrhythmic medications, destination therapy and device design (sdHR 1.94; 1.34-2.79 95% CI, p≤0.001). In contrast, there was no significant difference in mortality at 30-days or 2-years between patients with preoperative paroxysmal AF and those without preoperative AF (30-day mortality: 5.7% vs 6.4%, p=0.408; 2-year all-cause mortality: 27.2% vs 24.2%, p=0.010). The risk of long-term mortality was also not significantly different (sdHR 1.19; 0.95-1.5 95% CI, p=0.137). In conclusion, a preoperative history of persistent/permanent AF is associated with increased risk of mortality following LVAD implantation, but there is no significant difference in survival between patients with preoperative paroxysmal AF and those without AF.

title: Projected Demand for Cardiac Electrophysiology Procedures in Australia to 2040: A National Population-Based Modelling Study.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Cardiac electrophysiology services are expanding rapidly owing to an ageing population, increasing prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias, expanding indications for catheter ablation and cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) therapy, and continued advances in procedural technology. Despite this, the future demand for electrophysiology procedures has not been estimated.

METHODS: We conducted a national population-based forecasting study using Australian Institute of Health and Welfare hospital procedural data between 2010 and 2024. Catheter ablation and CIED procedures were identified using Australian Classification of Health Interventions procedure codes. Historical trends in procedural volume and population-adjusted utilisation were evaluated. Future procedural demand to 2040 was estimated using linear regression and generalised additive models.

RESULTS: Between 2010 and 2024, 612,302 cardiac electrophysiology procedures were performed in Australia. Annual procedural volume increased from 28,805 to 55,919 procedures, representing a 94.1% increase. Catheter ablation activity increased by 200.8%, compared with 60.9% for CIED procedures. Atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation demonstrated the greatest absolute increase in procedure volume (7,582 annual procedures, 471.8%), while ventricular ablation demonstrated the greatest proportional increase (1,862.7%) from a low baseline volume. Forecast modelling projected total electrophysiology procedural activity to increase to 80,185 procedures annually by 2040 (95% confidence interval [CI], 76,237-84,133), representing a 43.4% (95% CI, 36.3-50.5%) increase from 2024. Catheter ablation demand is projected to increase by 54.2%, compared to 37.1% for CIED procedures, with AF ablation accounting for the largest increase in future procedural demand.

CONCLUSIONS: Cardiac electrophysiology procedural demand in Australia is projected to increase substantially over the coming decades. The anticipated growth is driven predominantly by continued growth in catheter ablation, particularly AF ablation. These findings provide an evidence base to support planning of future electrophysiology workforce requirements, procedural infrastructure and healthcare resource allocation to ensure sufficient capacity to meet the growing demand for electrophysiology services.

title: Smartpatch long-term monitoring superior to 24-hour Holter for detecting idiopathic ventricular arrhythmia: a retrospective self-controlled study.
summary:
OBJECTIVE: To compare the diagnostic performance, patient comfort, and heart rate variability (HRV) assessment of a novel long-term Smartpatch monitor with those of a conventional 24-hour Holter monitor in patients with suspected idiopathic ventricular arrhythmia (IVA).

METHODS: This retrospective self-controlled study enrolled 164 patients who underwent simultaneous 24-hour Holter and 7- to 14-day Smartpatch monitoring. Detection rates of arrhythmia subtypes, premature ventricular contraction (PVC) burden, symptom-rhythm correlation, wearing comfort (assessed using 5-point Likert scale), HRV indices (SDNN, SDANN, RMSSD), and diagnostic accuracy were compared between different monitoring methods.

RESULTS: Compared with Holter monitoring, Smartpatch showed significantly higher detection rates for all arrhythmia subtypes (all P < 0.05). Among the 85 patients with negative Holter findings, Smartpatch provided an incremental diagnostic yield of 18.8% (16/85), resulting in changes in clinical management for 9 patients (5 receiving pharmacological therapy and 4 undergoing ablation). Smartpatch was associated with superior overall comfort scores (4.3 ± 0.5 vs 2.9 ± 0.9, P = 0.007), a lower premature termination rate (1.2% vs 5.5%, P = 0.035), a higher proportion of valid recording data (98.5% vs 96.2%, P < 0.001), and a mean wear duration of 13.2 days. HRV indices were significantly higher with Smartpatch monitoring than with Holter monitoring (P < 0.05). Diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy for IVA were 94.2%, 91.8%, and 93.1% with Smartpatch, respectively, compared with 78.5%, 85.4%, and 80.2% with Holter (P < 0.001, P = 0.013, P < 0.001, respectively).

CONCLUSION: In patients with suspected IVA, long-term Smartpatch monitoring demonstrated higher arrhythmia detection rates, improved diagnostic accuracy, enhanced HRV assessment, and better patient comfort compared with 24-hour Holter monitoring. These findings support its use as a valuable tool for screening and diagnosis in patients with suspected IVA.

title: Unexpected Non-immune Hydrops Foetalis With Supraventricular Tachycardia in a Premature Neonate.
summary: Hydrops foetalis (HF) refers to abnormal excessive fluid collection in foetal compartments. We present a case of unexpected non-immune HF (NIHF) in a male neonate born at 31 weeks of gestation via emergency caesarean section. He was born cyanotic with absent breathing effort and heart rate, and was noted to have generalised oedema, a tense abdomen, and a puffy chest wall consistent with HF. Following initial resuscitation and intubation, he developed supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), which was reversed following administration of three incremental doses of adenosine. Biochemical evaluation revealed significant hypoalbuminaemia, and initial blood gas showed marked acidosis. Lung ultrasound demonstrated bilateral pleural effusions, and an emergency echocardiogram showed a mild pericardial effusion with a small patent foramen ovale. After transfer to the tertiary centre, he had recurrent episodes of SVT requiring multiple doses of adenosine and initiation of propranolol and flecainide. A total of 220 mL of ascitic fluid was drained, but no pleural drain was required. He subsequently improved clinically and was discharged on maintenance amiodarone and propranolol. This case demonstrates the importance of thorough assessment in neonates with NIHF to identify potentially treatable underlying causes, such as SVT. A detailed assessment to identify underlying aetiology and complications is essential, with management guided by these findings. Early diagnosis and treatment, along with effective resuscitation, can rapidly improve haemodynamic stability and outcomes.

title: The Inflammation-Electrical Remodeling Axis in the Infarct Border Zone: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Translation for Post-MI Ventricular Arrhythmias.
summary: Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) and sudden cardiac death (SCD) remain leading causes of mortality after myocardial infarction (MI). The conventional fibrosis-centric paradigm explains chronic reentrant VAs but cannot fully account for electrical instability in acute and subacute post-MI phases, highlighting an unmet need for upstream therapies targeting the arrhythmogenic substrate. Accumulating preclinical mechanistic and observational clinical evidence indicates that the inflammatory microenvironment in the infarct border zone may function as a critical upstream driver of electrical remodeling, mediated by neutrophils, macrophages and key pro-inflammatory cytokines (interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α)), constituting an inflammation-electrical remodeling axis that contributes to VA susceptibility across all post-MI stages. While causal relationships have been established in animal models, direct confirmation in human myocardium remains limited. This narrative review synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence on this axis. It summarizes its spatiotemporal dynamics, four core cellular and molecular mechanisms and the antiarrhythmic potential of diverse anti-inflammatory interventions. We further outline key evidence gaps and translational directions, including precision risk stratification and cell-type-specific targeted delivery. Based on preclinical and preliminary clinical evidence, targeting the inflammation-electrical remodeling axis represents a promising upstream strategy to reduce post-MI SCD by addressing the root causes of electrical instability, though definitive proof of efficacy in humans is pending, and dedicated randomized controlled trials with arrhythmia endpoints are still required for clinical validation.

title: Delayed Pericardial Tamponade After Left Ventricular Radiofrequency Ablation for Multifocal Premature Ventricular Complexes: A Case Report.
summary: Radiofrequency ablation has become an effective treatment for premature ventricular complexes (PVCs), but its potential for serious complications, particularly delayed pericardial tamponade, remains a concern. We report a 70-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cerebrovascular disease who presented with frequent, symptomatic, multifocal PVCs refractory to antiarrhythmic therapy. During the procedure, two morphological patterns of PVCs were identified using the ENSITE Precision Electroanatomic Mapping System (Medtronic). Ablation was performed sequentially at the left ventricular papillary muscle and the left ventricular posterolateral wall using a contact force sensing catheter (TactiCath), with power set at 40 W, temperature limit of 43°C, and contact force of 10-30 g. A total of 240 s of ablation was delivered at the papillary muscle site, and 180 s at the posterolateral wall. Anticoagulation was maintained with 8000 U of intravenous heparin. Approximately 1.5 h after the procedure, the patient developed sudden diaphoresis and profound hypotension. Bedside echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse, and urgent pericardiocentesis drained approximately 800 mL of grossly bloody fluid. A pericardial drain was placed, but the patient later experienced recurrent hemodynamic instability and cardiac arrest. Despite aggressive cardiopulmonary resuscitation, blood product transfusion, and chest tube drainage, the patient succumbed to circulatory failure. This case highlights that prolonged and repeated ablation at the left ventricular papillary muscle and posterolateral wall carries a substantial risk of delayed cardiac tamponade, even when immediate post-procedural hemodynamics appear stable. High clinical vigilance and routine point-of-care ultrasound monitoring are essential for early detection and management of this life-threatening complication.

title: Early Right Ventricular Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Lead Microdislodgement Associated With Active-Fixation Helix Retraction: A Case Report.
summary: Lead dislodgement is an important early complication of cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) implantation, and microdislodgement may be clinically significant despite little or no visible change in lead position on standard radiography. We report the case of an 87-year-old man with ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, previous transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), and a pre-existing right-sided pacemaker for high-degree atrioventricular block. A dual-chamber implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) was implanted for secondary prevention after syncope associated with ventricular tachycardia. The newly implanted right ventricular (RV) defibrillator lead had satisfactory acute electrical parameters. Within the following days, the patient developed recurrent symptoms, slow ventricular tachycardia, and dynamic RV lead dysfunction evident during upper-limb mobilization. Device interrogation before lead revision showed an elevated RV pacing threshold, reduced R-wave amplitude to 2-3 mV, and an increase in lead impedance to 1500 Ω. Retraction of the active-fixation screw was identified. A few days after implantation, a new RV defibrillator lead was positioned at the RV apex, after which the dysfunctional lead was removed. Subsequent device follow-up was reassuring, with no recurrent RV lead dysfunction documented at long-term follow-up. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of early ICD lead microdislodgement and the value of integrating symptoms, device interrogation, telemetry, imaging, and dynamic mechanical assessment.

title: Successful atrial leadless pacemaker implantation in an 11-year-old with congenital sinus node dysfunction: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Sinus node dysfunction (SND) is rare in the paediatric population. Leadless atrial pacing represents a novel therapeutic option. To our knowledge, this case represents the youngest reported patient to receive an atrial leadless pacemaker (AVEIR AR). While ventricular leadless pacing has been described in children, atrial leadless pacing experience in this population remains extremely limited.

CASE SUMMARY: An 11-year-old boy with lifelong bradycardia documented since fetal life presented with exertional dyspnoea and recurrent syncopal episodes. Electrocardiography revealed nodal rhythm without sinus activity. Electrophysiological evaluation demonstrated a corrected sinus node recovery time of 4800 ms and absence of chronotropic response to intravenous atropine (0.04 mg/kg IV). The patient met Class I criteria for permanent pacemaker implantation according to current paediatric pacing consensus recommendations, given symptomatic SND with chronotropic incompetence. An AVEIR AR leadless pacemaker was successfully implanted at the base of the right atrial appendage with optimal electrical parameters. No procedural or 18-month follow-up complications were observed.

DISCUSSION: This case demonstrates procedural feasibility of atrial leadless pacing in a carefully selected paediatric patient, with encouraging mid-term follow-up. Larger studies are required to establish long-term safety and clinical outcomes.

title: Complete Atrioventricular Block Revealing Late-onset Cardiac Fabry Disease: Diagnostic Role of Native T1 Mapping.
summary: A 63-year-old man presented with symptomatic complete atrioventricular block requiring urgent pacemaker implantation. Evaluation revealed non-obstructive left ventricular hypertrophy with normal coronary arteries. Cardiac magnetic resonance showed diffusely reduced native T1 values and inferolateral late gadolinium enhancement, suggesting Fabry cardiomyopathy; amyloidosis was excluded by bone scintigraphy. Diagnosis was confirmed by markedly reduced alpha-galactosidase A activity, elevated lyso-Gb3, and a pathogenic hemizygous GLA variant (p.Asn215Ser). Enzyme replacement therapy with agalsidase beta was initiated, with early stabilization of myocardial deformation and septal thickness. This case highlights native T1 mapping as a key diagnostic biomarker in unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Algorithm for Detection of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Compared with a Standard Electrocardiogram.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) may facilitate detection of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), but its ability to identify higher-risk patients undergoing clinical evaluation for HCM remains uncertain.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic performance of a commercially available AI-ECG algorithm among patients undergoing cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) for suspected or established HCM.

METHODS: We studied 102 patients with HCM and 302 age-, sex-, and year-matched controls without HCM who underwent clinically indicated CMR. An AI-ECG algorithm was applied to the first available ECG preceding CMR. Diagnostic performance, incremental value beyond standard ECG features, and associations with clinical outcomes were assessed.

RESULTS: ECGs preceded CMR by a median of 1.1 years. AI-ECG demonstrated moderate sensitivity (51.1%) and high specificity (96.1%) for identification of phenotypic HCM and incrementally improved discrimination and reclassification beyond demographic and conventional ECG variables (net reclassification improvement 0.19, p<0.001). Within one year of CMR, a positive AI-ECG was independently associated with the composite outcome (adjusted HR 2.68, 95% CI 1.42-5.09; p=0.003), driven by ICD placement and septal reduction therapy. Among patients with HCM, while exploratory, an AI-ECG probability ≥ 0.99 identified those at highest risk for subsequent events (HR 2.92, 95% CI 1.59-5.35; p=0.011).

CONCLUSION: In conclusion, among patients undergoing clinical evaluation for HCM, AI-ECG provided incremental diagnostic value beyond conventional ECG parameters and identified individuals at increased risk for subsequent treatment-related clinical outcomes.

title: ZGC Granules improve HFpEF complicated with atrial fibrillation by inhibiting proinflammatory and pro-fibrotic effects.
summary:
OBJECTIVE: This study investigated the efficacy and mechanism of Zhigancao Granules (ZGC) in improving outcomes in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) complicated by atrial fibrillation (AF), focusing on its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects.

METHOD: A total of 220 patients with HFpEF and AF were included and received conventional therapy alone (n = 109) or with ZGC Granules (n = 111) for 3 months, followed by 1-year follow-up. In vitro, HL-1 cardiomyocytes were stimulated with LPS plus palmitic acid and treated with ZGC (0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mg/mL). Cell viability was assessed by CCK-8; mRNA and protein expression of inflammatory and fibrotic markers were measured by qRT-PCR, ELISA, and Western blot.

RESULTS: The ZGC group showed significantly greater reductions in B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), C-reactive protein (CRP), Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), Interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-16, and Transforming growth factor-beta 1 (TGF-β1), along with significantly greater improvements in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class, 6-minute walk test (6MWT), Atrial Fibrillation Symptom Scale (AFSS), and Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome efficacy (90.99% vs. 78.90%, P < 0.05). At 1 year, the ZGC group had a lower readmission rate (18.02% vs. 28.83%, P < 0.05), while mortality and adverse events were similar between groups. In vitro, ZGC treatment restored cell viability and dose-dependently downregulated LPS/palmitic acid-induced inflammatory and fibrotic responses.

CONCLUSION: ZGC Granules improve cardiac function, exercise capacity, and inflammatory/fibrotic markers in HFpEF patients with AF, reduce readmission rates, and exhibit a favorable safety profile. Mechanistically, ZGC suppresses LPS/palmitic acid-induced inflammatory and fibrotic responses in cardiomyocytes, potentially through inhibition of NLRP3/Caspase-1 inflammasome activation.

title: Insights into Channelopathies and Sport: The Genotype-Positive/Phenotype-Negative Athlete from Molecular Diagnosis to Management.
summary: Channelopathies, diseases with ion channel perturbations, are a major cause of sudden cardiac death in athletes. Advances in genetic testing have identified a growing population of athletes carrying (likely) pathogenic variants in cardiac ion channel genes who remain phenotypically silent. These genotype-positive/phenotype-negative (G+/P-) individuals present a distinct clinical challenge. Standard preparticipation screening, designed around phenotypic findings, provides little guidance for their management. A critical gap exists in providing prognostic guidance based on the involved gene, specific variants, and its molecular consequences. Beyond a critical review of existing literature, we provide a mechanistically anchored framework for variant-specific arrhythmic risk stratification across the major channelopathy genes. For each gene, we translate molecular pathophysiology into clinically actionable risk profiles and examine how exercise-specific triggers, including adrenergic surge, electrolyte shifts, and sympathovagal imbalance, interact with the underlying molecular substrate to modulate arrhythmic vulnerability. Standard diagnostic tools ranging from electro- and echocardiography, exercise stress testing, and pharmacological provocation to emerging modalities such as electroanatomic mapping and magnetocardiography are evaluated for their capacity to unmask subclinical disease and refine sports eligibility decisions. The case for an interdisciplinary sports-cardio-genetic board is made alongside a call for international collaborative registries, as existing evidence in G+/P- athletes is largely absent. The integration of artificial intelligence and telemonitoring into longitudinal athletic surveillance is discussed as a pragmatic strategy for early phenotype detection. Ultimately, guidance for the G+/P- athlete rests on a thorough understanding of the causative genetic variant and its pathophysiological consequences.

title: ECG foundation models for cardiovascular screening in a cohort of young competitive athletes.
summary: AI-powered cardiac screening could evolve sports medicine by boosting accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness, with automated ECG interpretation based on foundation models becoming key for large-scale athlete screening. Before deployment, it is crucial to verify whether these clinically developed models are applicable to this population. We evaluated whether ECG foundation models trained on general clinical populations can diagnose athlete-specific ECG findings. We fine-tuned three models (ECG-FM, HuBERT-ECG, ECGFounder) on PhysioNet/CinC 2021, 87,662 samples, and tested them on 43 expert-annotated ECGs from highly trained/national-level athletes. Performance was strong on PhysioNet/CinC 2021 (AUROC 0.97, AUPRC 0.57, Sensitivity 0.89) but dropped on athletes' data, confirming domain shift. ECGFounder performed best (AUROC 0.84, AUPRC 0.72, Sensitivity 0.57) and detected the most frequent findings, Sinus Bradycardia (AUROC 0.87) and Sinus Arrhythmia (AUROC 0.95), well. Per-label estimates for rare classes must be interpreted cautiously, given the small cohort. This work contributes to developing athlete-focused AI frameworks for reliable ECG-based screening.
